decisions.why: The Latin closes the verse on the vocative Altíssime, a proparoxytone; the brief wants the last stress on the last or second-last syllable. Ps 9:3 (the same colon, psallam nómini tuo, Altíssime) moved the vocative to the head of the colon. Here the colon opens with 'e entoar', so the vocative goes inside, after the verb — which also keeps the Responsory's split (R. Bonum est confitéri Dómino, allelúja: * Et psállere, allelúja) whole: 'e entoar salmos' stands by itself. Draft 2 adds 'ó': without it the ambiguity reader heard 'Altíssimo' as an indirect object, not as the address.

options.label: , ó Altíssimo, ao vosso nome
options.note: draft 2 — the ambiguity reader heard the bare 'Altíssimo' as the one sung to ('to the Most High, to your name'); 'ó' marks the vocative

options.label: , Altíssimo, ao vosso nome
options.note: draft — vocative moved inside the colon; closes on 'nome'

options.label: ao vosso nome, Altíssimo
options.note: the Latin's order; the verse ends on a proparoxytone, as the Latin's does

options.label: ao vosso nome, ó Altíssimo
options.note: MS1932's 'ó Altíssimo'; same cadence problem

decisions.why: The DO Latin has a comma: two nouns, decachórdum (Lewis & Short: 'a musical instrument of ten strings', citing this very verse) and psaltérium; the Greek ἐν δεκαχόρδῳ ψαλτηρίῳ is one instrument, 'a ten-stringed psaltery' (MS1932 follows that). 'As dez cordas' keeps the Latin's noun (the ten-string thing) in one short phrase and still lets the ear take it as the psaltery's strings — the Latin's two readings both stay open. 'Com o instrumento de dez cordas' is +6 syllables; 'decacórdio' is a dictionary word no one knows. 'Com' for in + instrument follows 32:2 and 48:5. Draft 2: both the Latinist and the ambiguity reader heard 'as dez cordas' as strings, not an instrument; DRB's wording taken, at +6 syllables (sayable in one breath).

options.label: Com o instrumento de dez cordas, com o saltério

forms.decachordo: Com o instrumento de dez cordas, com o saltério

options.note: DRB 'upon an instrument of ten strings, upon the psaltery'; +6 syllables — draft 2: the Latinist (minor) — decachórdum is the instrument, not its strings; the ambiguity reader heard only ten strings

options.label: Com as dez cordas, com o saltério

forms.decachordo: Com as dez cordas, com o saltério

options.note: draft — two nouns as the DO Latin punctuates, the first named by its strings

forms.decachordo: Com o saltério de dez cordas

options.note: one instrument, as the Greek and MS1932; = 32:2's wording for in psaltério decem chordárum

options.label: No decacórdio, no saltério
options.note: the Latinist's own fix (with 'na cítara'); refused — 'decacórdio' is a dictionary word no one knows

decisions.why: Factúra (ποίημα, 'a thing made') is a second word beside ópera (ἔργα) in the same verse, so it should not also be 'obra' (MS1932 merges them: 'com as tuas obras … com as obras'). The cognate 'feitura' is exact but is heard as Bible-speak or as 'the making of' something. The clause 'o que fizestes' keeps the root of fácere, stays apart from 'obras', and is how D16 handled a noun Portuguese has no plain word for. Draft 2 takes the cognate 'feitura' (the Latinist); the clause stays an option.

options.label: com a vossa feitura
options.note: the exact cognate; rare in this sense — draft 2: the Latinist (minor) — the noun kept as a noun; the stylist also refused the clause (vaguer, and a chime -astes / -estes)

options.label: na vossa feitura
options.note: the v2 Latinist (minor): the Latin's in, parallel with 'nas obras' — held: the causative 'alegrar alguém em' is not how Portuguese builds it ('alegrar-se em' is the reflexive), and 'com' is the instrument the delectáre rows use (29:2, 64:8)

options.label: com o que fizestes
options.note: draft — the noun as a clause of the same root

options.label: com a vossa obra
options.note: plain, but merges factúra with ópera in the next colon; the stylist's proposal, refused: it makes one word of factúra and ópera, which the Latin (and the Greek ποίημα / ἔργα) keep apart

decisions.why: Magnificáre → engrandecer (glossary). The Latin perfect passive (ἐμεγαλύνθη) says the works have become great; the second colon says the thoughts 'factæ sunt' deep — two verbs of becoming. 'Como se engrandeceram' keeps the verb and matches 'se tornaram' in the second colon. 'Foram engrandecidas' keeps the voice but is heard as 'have been praised' (by men). 'Como são grandes' (DRB) drops the verb. The colon is also the Sunday Vespers short responsory (Quam magnificáta sunt * ópera tua, Dómine): 'Como se engrandeceram * as vossas obras, Senhor' divides there cleanly.

options.label: Como se engrandeceram
options.note: draft — the verb kept, as a verb of becoming

options.label: Como foram engrandecidas
options.note: the Latin passive to the letter

options.label: Como são grandes
options.note: DRB 'how great are thy works'; the verb lost

decisions.why: Nimis here is σφόδρα, the Greek of valde: 'muito', as the nimis row does at 47:2 and 118:96 ('sem medida' is kept for places where 'beyond measure' is the sense). Factæ sunt → 'se tornaram' (the fíeri row's word for a state that came about).

decisions.why: Cognóscere with no object of its own (hæc comes only at the end of the second colon). The glossary's rule: 'conhecer' wants an object, so 13:4 Nonne cognóscent omnes took 'saber'. 'Não saberá' is how Portuguese says 'will not know' absolutely; 'não conhecerá' keeps the row's verb and can take hæc as a shared object.

options.note: draft — as 13:4

options.label: conhecerá
options.note: the row's verb; MS1932 'não conhecerá'

decisions.latin: Cum exórti fúerint peccatóres sicut fænum
decisions.why: Exóriri is 'rise, spring up' (ἀνατεῖλαι, used of the sun and of plants); with grass beside it the plant's sense is the one the image makes. 'Brotar' is MS1932's word and says it concretely. The future perfect is given as the Portuguese future subjunctive (grammar).

options.note: draft; MS1932 'tiverem brotado'

options.note: keeps the 'rising' of the verb, loses the plant

decisions.why: The fænum row splits by what the verse does: hay where it dries (36:2 'feno'), grass where it grows (71:16 'erva', after two readers refused flowering hay). Here it springs up: 'erva'.

options.note: draft — the row's word for growing grass; MS1932 'a erva'

options.label: o feno
options.note: the row's other word; wrong for springing up

decisions.why: 91:8 is a when-clause with no main verb; the Latin answers it with a bare purpose clause (Cum … : Ut intéreant — '[it is] that they may perish'). Portuguese needs the copula to make it a sentence ('Quando … : é para que …'); a copula is what D2 lets the ear supply. Without it the purpose clause hangs. MS1932 instead supplies a new verb ('imediatamente perecerão'), which changes the Latin. Draft 2 returns to the Latin's bare clause, on two readers' remarks.

options.label: Para que
options.note: the Latin's bare clause (DRB 'That they may perish') — draft 2: the Latinist (minor) — the copula settled a link the Latin leaves loose; the ambiguity reader could not tell what 'É' referred to

options.label: É para que
options.note: draft — the copula supplied

decisions.why: Interíre (ἐξολεθρευθῶσιν, the Greek behind both disperíre and interíre in Ps 36) → 'extinguir-se' by the disperíre / interíre row (36:38 'se extinguirá'); 'morrer' is for a man's death (48:18). It stays apart from períre → 'perecer', which follows in the next verse (períbunt).

options.note: draft — the row's word

options.label: pereçam
options.note: DRB, MS1932 'perish'; merges with períbunt in 91:10; the Latinist's fix (minor) — refused: the interíre row keeps 'extinguir-se', so that intéreant and períbunt (91:10) stay two verbs as in the Latin

decisions.latin: tu autem Altíssimus in ætérnum, Dómine
decisions.why: Altíssimus is the predicate. 'O Altíssimo' makes it the divine name, echoing the vocative Altíssime of 91:2; 'altíssimo' (DRB 'most high') makes it a description. The Greek ὕψιστος is both. The name is kept for the echo; the Latin order keeps the vocative last, so the verse ends on 'Senhor'.

options.label: o Altíssimo
options.note: draft; MS1932 'és eternamente o Altíssimo'

options.label: altíssimo
options.note: the adjective, DRB 'art most high'

decisions.why: Unicórnis is nominative or genitive (the forms are the same); the Greek μονοκέρωτος is genitive, 'as a unicorn's'. 'Como o do unicórnio' takes that reading, the one DRB and MS1932 take; 'como um unicórnio' compares the horn with the whole animal. The unicorn stays (the unicórnis row). Draft 2 puts the verb first, the Latin's order (the stylist: it eases the run-up to the mediant).

options.label: como o do unicórnio
options.note: draft — MS1932 'como a do unicórnio'

options.label: como o de um unicórnio
options.note: indefinite

options.label: como um unicórnio
options.note: the nominative reading

decisions.latin: et senéctus mea in misericórdia úberi
decisions.why: The second colon has no verb: exaltábitur carries over. The Latin reads misericórdia where the Greek has ἐλαίῳ ('in rich oil' — ἐλαίῳ / ἐλέει); the Latin is followed (rule 1). The ellipsis is kept, with a comma to mark it; supplying 'estará' would say what the Latin leaves to the first verb.

options.label: , em misericórdia
options.note: draft 2 — the stylist: 'numa' conversational; 'em' plainer, and 91:15 follows ('em velhice fecunda')

options.label: , numa misericórdia
options.note: draft — ellipsis kept

options.note: a verb supplied

options.label: na misericórdia
options.note: DRB 'and my old age in plentiful mercy'

decisions.latin: in misericórdia úberi · in senécta úberi
decisions.why: The same adjective twice (úber: 'rich, fruitful, fertile, abundant' — Lewis & Short; from 'udder'; the Greek πίων, 'fat'), so one word for both (rule 6). 'Fecunda' fits both: MS1932 has 'velhice fecunda', and the fruitfulness belongs to a psalm of trees that flower and multiply. 'Abundante' is right for mercy but odd for old age; 'farta' (ubértas → fartura, 35:9) is odd for both; 'rica' would make the old age wealthy. Draft 2: 'em' without the article in both places (the stylist).

options.label: fecunda
options.note: draft — one word for both places

options.label: abundante
options.note: DRB 'plentiful mercy'; odd with velhice

options.note: the ubértas row's root

decisions.latin: Et despéxit óculus meus inimícos meos
decisions.why: The same words as 53:9 (despéxit óculus meus), which reads 'o meu olho olhou de cima para os meus inimigos'; here the accusative takes 117:7's build without 'para'. The despícere (enemies) row keeps both the literal 'look down on' and its contempt. The jingle 'olho olhou' is the row's known cost, accepted at 53:9; 'viu de cima' is the row's alternative. The v1 stylist named 91:12 the worst line for the jingle; held for 53:9's sake, and flagged in the glossary row: if Gustavo lifts it, 53:9 and 91:12 change together.

options.label: viu de cima
options.note: the row's alternative, against the jingle

options.label: viu do alto
options.note: the stylist, against the 'olho olhou' jingle (his worst line) — refused: the same Latin as 53:9 (despéxit óculus meus) keeps the same Portuguese (rule 6); the jingle is the row's known cost

options.label: olhou com desprezo para
options.note: MS1932; the contempt only

decisions.latin: et in insurgéntibus in me malignántibus áudiet auris mea
decisions.why: The Latin gives no object to 'hear': in + ablative, 'in the case of / concerning' the malignant who rise against me. DRB supplies 'the downfall'; MS1932 'ouvirão falar (sem medo)'. 'Ouvir dos malvados' is 'hear of' and also 'hear from' — both open, and nothing supplied. Malignántes → malvados (D24); insúrgere in → levantar-se contra. Draft 2 puts the subject first (the stylist: 'o meu ouvido ouvirá dos malvados'), so the two echoes of the verse are further apart and the colon ends on 'mim'. The ambiguity reader heard 'hear the wicked themselves' — one of the two readings the Latin leaves open. The v2 Latinist (minor) asked 'acerca dos' as clearer, granting that 'de' can carry the sense; held, because 'acerca' closes the openness of the Latin's in, which the draft keeps on purpose.

options.label: dos malvados
options.note: draft — nothing supplied

options.label: acerca dos malvados
options.note: 'concerning', the one reading; the v2 Latinist's fix (minor), held

options.label: a queda dos malvados
options.note: DRB's supplied 'downfall' — refused: says what the Latin does not

decisions.why: The Latin order keeps the two colons parallel — comparison, then verb: 'como a palmeira florescerá: * como o cedro do Líbano se multiplicará' — and both colons end on an oxytone future. The plain order 'O justo florescerá como a palmeira' is the familiar line and is the option. The verse is said alone as a versicle (V. Justus ut palma florébit. R. Sicut cedrus Líbani multiplicábitur) and as the Introit of Doctors with 91:14's 'in domo Dómini'; both orders read alone.

options.label: O justo, como a palmeira, florescerá
options.note: draft — the Latin's order

options.label: O justo florescerá como a palmeira
options.note: natural order; MS1932

decisions.why: Palma is the tree (φοῖνιξ, the date palm). In Brazil 'palma' is first the palm of the hand or a palm branch (and a cactus in the northeast); 'palmeira' is the tree.

options.label: palmeira
options.note: draft

options.label: palma
options.note: the cognate; MS1932

decisions.why: Multiplicári → multiplicar-se (glossary), twice in the psalm, so one verb. Of a single cedar it is strange (DRB turns it 'grow up', from the Hebrew's sense); the Latin (πληθυνθήσεται) says multiply, and in 91:15 the just in the plural 'multiply' in old age. Kept. The ambiguity reader heard 'grow / increase' first — the sense passed.

options.note: draft — the row's verb; MS1932

options.label: crescerá / crescerão
options.note: DRB 'grow up'; another verb (créscere)

decisions.why: Bene patiéntes is a calque of εὐπαθοῦντες, 'faring well'; Lewis & Short give pati its sense 'to experience, be in a certain state'. A Latin ear can also hear 'enduring well' (a reading of patience is said to be Augustine's — from memory, unverified). Portuguese has no phrase that holds both; word for word ('bem sofrendo', 'bem pacientes') is not a sentence or says 'very patient'. The draft takes the sense the calque was made to carry, plainly and without adding (MS1932 'cheios de vigor' and DRB 'well treated' each add). Draft 2 takes 'passarão bem'. Risk to watch: 'passarão' heard as 'pass by'.

options.label: passarão bem
options.note: 'passar' as 'undergo', like pati; colloquial, and 'passarão' can be heard as 'pass by' — draft 2: the Latinist (minor) — a verb of faring keeps the participle of pati; the stylist and the ambiguity reader found 'estarão bem' flat ('they'll be fine')

decisions.why: Quóniam here is 'that' (ut annúntient quóniam — announce that), continuing 91:15. 'Que o Senhor, nosso Deus, é reto' is a plain content clause. With the Latin's order, 'Que reto é o Senhor' is heard as an exclamation ('how upright the Lord is!'), which the Latin is not. The Latin's noster is followed against the Greek μου.

options.label: Que o Senhor, nosso Deus, é reto

choices.91:2: confitéri → dar graças a (D5); psállere → entoar salmos (D25). 'É bom' for Bonum est (not 'Bom é'), the natural order. The verse is the Offertory / Gradual of several Masses and a Responsory (R. Bonum est confitéri Dómino, allelúja: * Et psállere, allelúja); it reads alone. The switch from 'Dómino' (third person) to 'nómini tuo' (second) is the Latin's and is kept.
choices.91:3: annuntiáre → anunciar (D41); mane → de manhã (row); per noctem → durante a noite (the nox row's build, singular here). véritas → verdade (row), not the Hebrew-based 'fidelidade'. Read alone as a Gradual/Alleluia verse (Ad annuntiándum mane …): it does.
choices.91:4: in + instrument → com, as 32:2 and 48:5; cum cántico → com cântico. The Latin's in / cum distinction is lost (grammar). The colon ends on 'cítara', a proparoxytone, as the Latin's ends on 'cíthara' — accepted as at 56:9. cíthara → cítara, psaltérium → saltério (rows). Draft 2: 'com o cântico' (the stylist — the article, as with the three instruments around it).
choices.91:5: delectáre (causative, εὔφρανας) → alegrar, as 29:2 and 64:8 (the delectári row). exsultáre in → exultar em (row). The Latin's verb-last order kept in the second colon: it ends on an oxytone.
choices.91:6: cogitátio → pensamento (row; this verse named there).
choices.91:7: vir → homem; insípiens → insensato, stultus → tolo (D43; 48:11 has the pair: 'o insensato e o tolo'); intellégere → entender.
choices.91:8: apparére → aparecer; operári iniquitátem → praticar a iniquidade (row, = 91:10). The verse ends on a colon: its sentence runs into 91:9.
choices.91:9: in sǽculum sǽculi → pelos séculos dos séculos (D27); in ætérnum → para sempre (D23).
choices.91:10: The Latin's repetition 'quóniam ecce inimíci tui … quóniam ecce inimíci tui' kept whole, vocative and all. ecce → eis (que); períre → perecer; dispérgere (people) → dispersar, passive, as 58:16. Long verse, as the Latin's.
choices.91:11: cornu → chifre (row), exaltáre → exaltar (row: 74:11 'serão exaltados os chifres do justo'). senéctus → velhice. The ambiguity reader heard the cuckold's 'chifre' and a mythical unicorn: both rows keep the Latin's image unexplained (as 74:11, 21:22).
choices.91:12: óculus singular → o meu olho (row); auris → o meu ouvido (singular, as the Latin). The tenses are the Latin's: perfect despéxit, future áudiet. The past / future sequence the ambiguity reader found jarring is the Latin's (despéxit … áudiet).
choices.91:13: cedrus Líbani → o cedro do Líbano (36:35 'os cedros do Líbano').
choices.91:14: 'na casa do Senhor … nos átrios da casa do nosso Deus' = the formula of 133:1b / 134:2 (átrium → átrio, domus → casa).
choices.91:15: senécta → velhice (as senéctus in 91:11; 70:18). adhuc → ainda (41:6b). ut annúntient → para que anunciem; the verse ends on a colon, its object is 91:16.
choices.91:16: rectus → reto; iníquitas → iniquidade (row), where the Greek has ἀδικία.

audit.note: Latin = DO Psalm91.txt (15 prayed verses, 91:2–91:16; no titulus, D7).

Psalm-level draft from consult/parallels/ps091.md. Hard readings: 91:4 decachórdum as a noun (L&S cites this verse); 91:5 factúra beside ópera; 91:8–9 the when-clause answered by a bare purpose clause; 91:11 misericórdia where the Greek has 'oil' (followed, rule 1), and the verbless second colon; 91:12 'hear' with no object; 91:15 bene patiéntes (calque of εὐπαθοῦντες). Liturgical pieces checked by grep in content/do (Latin): 91:2 (Offertory, Responsory), 91:3 (Gradual verse), 91:6a (Sunday Vespers short responsory Quam magnificáta sunt * ópera tua, Dómine), 91:13 (versicle; with 91:14's in domo Dómini the Introit/Gradual of Commune C4a, C5).

Draft 1: hard pass. Soft, all accepted: 91:2b +3 (the vocative moved inside the colon; two-word 'entoar salmos', D25's known cost); 91:3b +3 ('durante a noite' for per noctem); 91:5b −4 (Portuguese is shorter than 'opéribus mánuum tuárum'); 91:7b +4 ('estas coisas' for hæc); 91:9a +5 (the supplied copula and the reflexive 'se extingam'); 91:11a +3 ('como o do' for the genitive); 91:13a +5 (the article and 'palmeira'). 91:4b closes on the proparoxytone 'cítara', as the Latin closes on 'cíthara' (as 56:9). No rhyme flags.
